intro: Every day the dice roll a premise and a dozen constraints, and the game has to honour all of them. Today's roll was seed 150807326. Here is each roll and what became of it.

rolls.value: 🛥️ a motor boat with an intern
rolls.became: Tuppence, a little red motor boat on Lake Linden, and Pim, its intern, who is paid in pennies and thanked in nothing. Tuppence can't talk (it's a boat), so Pim does the talking, and the diving, and the dusting, and eventually the needlework.
On Lake Linden the lake folk row by and pay a penny a look at a shining pearl, but never at a gritty one. So the pearls on Tuppence's deck need dusting, constantly, because of the Wind.

As everyone on Lake Linden knows, two pearls of a size, dusted together and put to bed in one mussel, wake up as one pearl a size finer. So you drag a pearl onto its twin. Sixteen sizes, from Seed to Rice, Pea, Button, Thimble, Cherry, Plum, all the way up to a Cottage and then a Moon.

rolls.value: limited space to arrange · a reset loop
rolls.became: The deck only has so many mussel cups, so you're always short of room. And the reset is the Pearl Fair: take your best pearl across the lake, come home with ribbons, start a new summer with an empty deck.

The West Wind, a cloud with cheeks, who loves sails and cannot abide an engine. It blows grit down every row of Tuppence's deck from the west, so the first pearl in each row gets it. A cheap pearl upwind shields the good ones behind it.

Regina, the tall white yacht who has won the Pearl Fair every year anyone can remember, and calls engines smelly. Whatever pearl you bring, Regina's is exactly one size bigger. Nobody knows how. (The Wind knows how.)

rolls.value: the core action gets a new verb
rolls.became: After the first Fair, Pim takes up a needle, and dragging a pearl gets a second meaning: drop it on its chalk outline in the embroidery hoop and it's sewn on. Sewn pearls stop earning pennies but make every pearl shine brighter, forever, through every Fair.
Five pieces of needlework, twenty pearls to sew, and a few summers of Fairs. When you're away, the Wind takes a nap and Pim keeps diving and matchmaking at a fifth of the speed.
Pennies from the lake folk run into the millions by the end. The other number that runs away is the size of the pearls: by the end there's a pearl as big as a cottage, then one as big as the Moon.

Everything is thread on linen: satin-stitched pearls, running-stitch waves, French knots for smoke, cross-stitch grit, and a wooden embroidery hoop. Bubblegum 16 is very bright, so the lake is very bright.

Tuppence's Lullaby: a music box rocking in 3/4 in G major pentatonic, with a soft harp joining once Pim starts sewing and strings near the end. Every pluck and chime in the game is on the same five notes.
Once upon a time, on Lake Linden… The narrator takes everything completely seriously, especially the porridge for the mussels.

Pim's needlework grows from a handkerchief to a napkin, a tablecloth, a bedsheet, and then something very large, all hung on the washing line where the Wind keeps tugging at it. When the last pearl is sewn, Pim runs it up the flagpole: it was a sail all along. And the Wind, who can't resist a sail, changes sides on the spot.

Once the sail is up, you don't do anything else. The Wind blows the grit off every pearl, rolls the whole deck together into one Great Pearl, and fills the sail all the way to the Fair. Regina's sails go slack, and Tuppence putters back to tow Regina in. The engine was useful after all. It smells rather nice, actually.

outro: None of this was planned as one idea. It's twelve dice and a lot of saying yes.
